# Magga Saṁyutta (SN 45)
**ID:** SN 45
**Section:** Saṁyuttanikāya (sn)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Maggasaṁyutta* (SN 45), the opening section of the *Mahāvagga* of the *Saṁyuttanikāya*, is dedicated to the Noble Eightfold Path (*ariya aṭṭhaṅgika magga*), the foundational "middle way" in Buddhist practice [Norman 1983; SuttaCentral]. While cataloged as containing 180 discourses, much of its numerical extent consists of formulaic repetition series (*peyyāla*), including the *Gaṅgā-peyyāla*, *Appamāda-*, *Balakaraṇīya-*, *Esanā-*, and *Ogha-vagga* (S V 38–62) [SuttaCentral; Gethin 2001]. The commentary (*Sāratthappakāsinī*) and manuscript colophons establish that these repetition series in the *Maggasaṁyutta* provide the structural and stylistic template expanded in subsequent *saṁyuttas* of the *Mahāvagga*, such as the *Bojjhaṅga-*, *Indriya-*, and *Jhānasaṁyutta* (*yathā Maggasamyuttaṁ evaṁ...*) [Norman 1983; Gethin 2001].
The collection defines the eight path factors systematically, beginning with right view (*sammādiṭṭhi*), explained as direct knowledge of the Four Noble Truths, progressing through virtue and mental training, and culminating in right immersion (*sammāsamādhi*) and the four *jhānas* [Anderson 1999; SuttaCentral]. A central doctrinal discourse is the *Magga-vibhaṅga Sutta* (SN 45.8), which details each step of the path, including the components of right speech and right view [Anderson 1999; Pa Auk Sayadaw et al. 2009]. Another celebrated discourse is the *Upaḍḍhasutta* (SN 45.2), in which the Buddha corrects Ānanda's assertion that good companionship is half of the spiritual life, declaring instead that admirable friendship (*kalyāṇamittatā*) constitutes the entirety of the holy life (*brahmacariya*) [Global Recovery 2010; SuttaCentral]. Other discourses employ similes, such as the diverse winds blowing across the sky, to illustrate how the path brings the four establishments of mindfulness to fulfillment [Gethin 2001].
Curated parallels on SuttaCentral link 27 suttas of SN 45 to extensive non-Pali parallels, foremost among them 24 discourses in the Chinese *Saṁyuktāgama* (T 99) (e.g., SĀ 749 to SN 45.1, SĀ 726 and SĀ 768 to SN 45.2, and SĀ 770, SĀ 784, and T 112 to SN 45.21) [SuttaCentral; Tsukamoto 1979]. Additional parallels exist in the Tibetan Kangyur (D 300, *Kalyāṇa-mitra-sevana-sūtra* to SN 45.2), the *Madhyama Āgama* (MĀ 141), and the Sanskrit *Arthaviniścayasūtra* [SuttaCentral]. In agreement with these links, DharmaNexus identifies substantial cross-language alignments with T 99 (fascicles 18, 27, and 28) and the *Arthaviniścayasūtra*, alongside citations in the *Vyākhyāyuktiṭīkā* and *Abhidharmasamuccaya* [DharmaNexus]. Internally within the Pali canon, DharmaNexus calculates over 27,000 matching passages across 384 texts, with its largest textual overlaps found in the repetitive formulas of SN 46, SN 48, SN 50, the *Paṭisambhidāmagga* (Ps 3.4), and ten-factor path parallels in the *Aṅguttaranikāya* (AN 10) [DharmaNexus; Gethin 2001].
